edges.effect_quant: In a randomized crossover trial of 32 people with self-identified aspartame-related headaches, headaches were reported on 33% of aspartame days versus 24% of placebo days (p = 0.04), with the largest difference in participants who were very sure they were sensitive; in a later double-blind crossover study of 48 self-identified sensitive individuals and 48 matched controls, no symptom differences were found between aspartame and control bars.
edges.population: adults with self-reported headache or migraine susceptibility, especially people who believe aspartame triggers their symptoms
edges.mechanism: If a real trigger effect exists, it may relate to susceptible individuals responding to phenylalanine-, neurotransmitter-, or stress-related pathways after aspartame ingestion, but placebo and nocebo effects clearly complicate this literature.
edges.summary: Aspartame does not appear to provoke headaches reliably in the general population, but a subset of self-identified sensitive individuals may experience more headaches under blinded challenge. The fairest reading is mixed evidence with a possible susceptible subgroup rather than a universal trigger effect.
edges.caveats: The positive trial was small and had attrition, whereas the later negative study tested acute symptom responses with a different protocol and broader psychological phenotyping. Self-reported trigger beliefs and expectancy effects are major confounders in this literature.

evidence.notes: Aspartame ingestion and headaches: a randomized crossover trial.

evidence.citation: Trefz FK et al 2015 PLoS One
